lead: A jet that strikes a vane changes direction, and its momentum changes. The vane feels a force. The force is largest when the jet is turned back on itself, and it falls when the vane moves away because the jet meets the vane more slowly. This chapter derives that force for flat plates, curved vanes and a wheel with many vanes. The results feed directly into the Pelton wheel and every machine that uses a jet. Some syllabi call this impact of jet on flat and curved vanes.
prereq: You need: the linear momentum equation from Unit 3, Fluid Dynamics and Flow Measurement, and the definitions of density and area from Unit 1, Fluid Properties and Fluid Statics.

sections.h3: A stationary plate stops the jet

blocks.text: Water leaves a nozzle as a jet of area a (m²) and speed V (m/s). The mass reaching a stationary vane per second is ṁ = ρaV, where ρ is density (kg/m³) and ṁ is mass flow rate (kg/s). Take the jet direction as positive. The vane changes the jet's velocity, so the jet's momentum changes. The force on the vane is equal and opposite to the force that changes the jet's momentum.
For a flat plate held normal to the jet, the water leaves along the plate. It has no velocity left in the jet direction. Every kilogram loses velocity V, so the force is:

blocks.where: F is the force on the vane (N); ρ is density (kg/m³); a is jet area (m²); V is jet speed (m/s).

blocks.text: For a curved vane that turns the jet through angle θ, the leaving velocity has component V cos θ in the original direction. θ is the deflection angle, measured from the old jet direction to the new one. The force is:

blocks.where: θ is the angle through which the jet is deflected; cos θ uses the same angle unit as θ.

blocks.text: Put θ = 90° for a flat plate: cos 90° = 0, so F = ρaV². Put θ = 180° for a hemispherical cup: cos 180° = −1, so F = 2ρaV². The cup gets twice the force of a flat plate from the same jet. This is why turbine buckets are curved to turn water back, not just sideways. The force acts on the vane; the water feels the same force in the opposite direction.

sections.h3: A moving vane sees a slower jet

blocks.text: Now the vane moves away from the nozzle at speed u (m/s) along the jet. If u < V, the jet meets the vane at relative speed V − u. The mass striking one moving vane per second is ρa(V − u), not ρaV. After the turn, the relative speed is still V − u when friction is neglected. The change of absolute velocity in the jet direction is (V − u)(1 − cos θ). Hence:

blocks.where: u is vane speed (m/s); V − u is the relative speed at entry and exit (m/s); other symbols are as before.

blocks.text: For a moving flat plate, θ = 90°, so F = ρa(V − u)². If u = V, the jet never catches the plate, so F = 0. If u = 0, the formula returns the stationary result.

Work done per second is P = Fu, where P is power in watts (W). Vane efficiency is η = P/(½ρaV³). The denominator is the kinetic energy of the jet passing per second. For a single vane this η uses the whole jet's kinetic energy ½ρaV³ as the input; it is a convention, not the energy of the water that actually strikes the vane. For one 180° curved vane, P = 2ρa u(V − u)². This is zero at u = 0, rises to a peak at u = V/3, and returns to zero at u = V. A single vane is therefore not best at half speed; it is best at one-third speed.

sections.h3: Many vanes use the whole jet

blocks.text: In a wheel, one vane follows another. The jet is always hitting some vane, so all the water from the nozzle is deflected. The mass striking per second is the full ρaV. At entry the relative speed is V − u; at exit it is V − u in a new direction. The force is:

blocks.where: F is the force on the series of vanes (N); the mass flow is the full jet mass flow ρaV.

blocks.text: Work per second is P = Fu = ρaV(V − u)(1 − cos θ)u. Divide by ρaV³ and put x = u/V. Then P/(ρaV³) = (1 − cos θ)x(1 − x). For a 180° bucket, this is 2x(1 − x), a parabola. It peaks at x = 0.5, so u = V/2. That is the ideal bucket speed for a Pelton wheel; 6.4 uses this result. Vane efficiency is η = P/(½ρaV³); for the series this becomes 2(1 − cos θ)x(1 − x).

For u = 0 the series formula becomes ρaV²(1 − cos θ), the stationary curved vane. For θ = 90° it becomes ρaV(V − u), the flat-plate series result. The series arrangement gives more work than one vane because the full jet mass flow ρaV is deflected, while a single vane is struck only by ρa(V − u).

figure.caption: Work rate against speed ratio for a single moving flat plate, a single 180° curved vane and a series of vanes. The series curve peaks at u/V = 0.5; the single vane peaks near 0.33 and is lower.

spec.aria: Work rate against vane speed ratio for a single moving flat plate, a single 180° curved vane and a series of vanes; the single vane peaks near 0.33 and the series of vanes peaks at 0.5.

examples.question: A jet of water 40 mm in diameter leaves a nozzle at V = 25 m/s and strikes one curved vane. The vane moves in the jet direction at u = 10 m/s. The vane deflects the jet through θ = 120°. Friction is neglected and ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find the force on the vane and the work done per second.
steps: Diameter d = 40 mm = 0.04 m. Jet area a = πd²/4 = π(0.04)²/4 = 1.257 × 10⁻³ m².
Relative speed at inlet Vr = V − u = 25 − 10 = 15 m/s.
For one moving vane, F = ρaVr²(1 − cos θ).
Work per second P = Fu = 424 × 10 = 4240 W = 4.24 kW.
examples.answer: The force on the vane is about 424 N and the work done per second is 4.24 kW.
examples.check:
import math
rho = 1000
d = 0.04
V = 25
u = 10
theta = math.radians(120)
a = math.pi * d * d / 4
vr = V - u
F = rho * a * vr**2 * (1 - math.cos(theta))
P_kW = F * u / 1000
print(round(a, 6))
print(round(vr, 1))
print(round(F, 0))
print(round(P_kW, 2))

traps: Using the absolute jet speed V instead of the relative speed V − u for a moving vane. The jet meets the vane at V − u.
Dropping the (1 − cos θ) factor. A flat plate has θ = 90° and factor 1; a 180° cup has factor 2.
Mixing the single-vane and series formulas. One moving vane uses mass flow ρa(V − u); a series of vanes uses ρaV.
Forgetting that diameter is not area. Convert 40 mm to 0.04 m and then use a = πd²/4.
Reporting the force on the water as the force on the vane. The two are equal in size and opposite in direction.

quiz.q: Write the force on a stationary flat plate held normal to a jet of area a and speed V.
quiz.a: F = ρaV², where ρ is density, a is jet area and V is jet speed.

quiz.q: Why does a 180° cup feel twice the force of a flat plate from the same jet?
quiz.a: A flat plate has θ = 90°, so 1 − cos θ = 1. A 180° cup has θ = 180°, so 1 − cos θ = 2. The mass flow ρaV is the same, so the force doubles.

quiz.q: For one moving vane, why is the mass flow ρa(V − u) and not ρaV?
quiz.a: The vane runs away from the jet at speed u, so the jet meets it at relative speed V − u. Only the water that catches the vane in one second strikes it.

quiz.q: A jet with a = 0.002 m² and V = 20 m/s strikes a stationary curved vane with θ = 120°. Find the force.
A series of vanes has a = 0.0015 m², V = 30 m/s, u = 12 m/s and θ = 150°. Find the force.
Explain why the work curve for a series of vanes peaks at u/V = 0.5 while one 180° vane peaks at 1/3.
quiz.a: For one 180° vane, P ∝ u(V − u)²; its derivative gives V − 3u = 0, so u = V/3. For a series, P ∝ u(V − u); its derivative gives V − 2u = 0, so u = V/2.

quiz.q: At u = V, what is the force on one moving vane and on a series of vanes? Explain using mass flow.
quiz.a: Both forces are zero. For one vane, no water strikes because the relative speed is zero. For a series, water still passes, but its relative velocity is zero, so it changes no momentum.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same momentum balance sizes jet deflectors, descaling nozzles and Pelton buckets. CFD models add friction, air drag and free-surface effects that the (1 − cos θ) factor hides. Erosion by silt is studied with particle-laden jets.
